Labor and Industry Review Commission
Theresa A. Aronson Unemployment Insurance
Claimant Decision1
Dated and Mailed:
Hearing No. 20405108MD September 29, 2021

The commission modifies and, as modified, affirms in part and reverses in part the
appeal tribunal decision. Accordingly, the claimant is eligible for Pandemic
Unemployment Assistance (PUA) under section 2102(a)(3)(A)(ii)(I)(kk) of the CARES
Act for weeks 13 through 20 of 2020, if otherwise qualified.
By the Commission: /s/
Michael H. Gillick, Chairperson
/s/
Georgia E. Maxwell, Commissioner
/s/
Marilyn Townsend, Commissioner
1 Appeal Rights: See the blue enclosure for the time limit and procedures for obtaining judicial
review of this decision. If you seek judicial review, you must name the following as defendants in the
summons and the complaint: the Labor and Industry Review Commission, all other parties in the
caption of this decision or order (the boxed section above), and the Department of Workforce
Development. Appeal rights and answers to frequently asked questions about appealing an
unemployment insurance decision to circuit court are also available on the commission’s website,
http://lirc.wisconsin.gov.

Procedural Posture
This case is before the commission to consider the claimant’s eligibility for
Pandemic Unemployment Assistance (PUA). An administrative law judge (ALJ) of
the Unemployment Insurance Division of the Department of Workforce
Development held a hearing and issued a decision. The commission received a
timely petition for review. The commission has considered the petition, and it has
reviewed the evidence submitted at the hearing.
Findings of Fact and Conclusions of Law
1. The claimant was last employed on March 18, 2020 (week 12). She was self-
employed as a part-time cleaner for two apartment complexes.
2. The claimant worked 22 to 25 hours per week, because her plan was to go to
part-time retirement January 1, 2020. She only worked as much as she could
without her pay adversely affecting how much she receives in Social Security
benefits.
3. The claimant does not have a medical reason as to why she did not work more
than 25 hours per week.
4. On March 12, 2020 (week 11), Governor Evers issued Executive Order #72, in
which he declared that a public health emergency exists in the state due to the
spread of COVID-19. All state agencies were ordered to assist in the response
to the public emergency.
5. On March 13, 2020, Governor Evers directed the Department of Health
Services Secretary-designee Andrea Palm to issue an order mandating
statewide closure of all public and private schools effective at 5 p.m. on March
18 (week 12).
6. On March 18, 2020 (week 12), Governor Evers issued Emergency Order #7,
which modified the eligibility requirements for individuals seeking
unemployment insurance benefits during the COVID-19 pandemic concerning
their ability to work, availability for work, and obligation to search for work.
7. On March 24, 2020 (week 13), the state issued a Safer at Home Order,
Emergency Order #12. All individuals in Wisconsin were ordered to stay at
home, with outlined exceptions. All non-essential businesses and operations
were ordered to cease all activities, except for minimum basic operations and
operations where employees could work from home. All essential businesses
and operations were encouraged to remain open. On April 25, 2020 (week 17),
the state’s second Safer at Home Order, Emergency Order #28, went into effect
upon the expiration of the first.
8. The primary place at which the claimant cleaned was shut down when the first
Safer at Home Order was issued in week 13 of 2020.
9. On Saturday, May 9, 2020 (week 19), the Department of Workforce
Development issued an emergency rule pertaining to the requirements for
individuals seeking unemployment insurance benefits during the COVID-19

pandemic with respect to an individual’s ability to work, availability for work,
and obligation to search for work. These rules supplanted Emergency Order #7,
which went into effect in week 12 of 2020. The new rule is applied beginning
with week 20 of 2020.
10. On Wednesday, May 13, 2020 (week 20), the Wisconsin Supreme Court struck
down the second Safer at Home Order, invalidating all provisions other than
mandated school closures.
11. The claimant was unable to return to work in May 2020, because she was
home-schooling her two grandchildren while their father worked.
12. The claimant was eligible for PUA for weeks 13 through 20 of 2020, if
otherwise qualified.
Memorandum Opinion
As a general rule, to be eligible for unemployment insurance benefits as to any
given week, a claimant must be able to work, available for work, and actively
seeking work during the week.2 “Able to work” means that the claimant maintains
an attachment to the labor market and has the physical and psychological ability to
engage in some substantial gainful employment in suitable work.3 “Available for
work” means that the claimant maintains an attachment to the labor market and is
ready to perform full-time suitable work in the labor market.4 “Full-time work”
means work performed for 32 hours or more per week.5 However, an individual with
a physical or psychological restriction will not be considered unavailable for work
solely because of his or her inability to work full-time, provided the individual is
available for suitable work for the number of hours the individual is able to work.6
A claimant is not available for suitable work if he or she has withdrawn from the
labor market due to restrictions on his or her availability for work.7 Suitable work is
defined as work that is reasonable considering the claimant’s training, experience,
and duration of unemployment as well as the availability of jobs in the labor
market.8
The unemployment insurance program is intended to provide temporary wage
insurance for individuals who are able to work and available for work but are
unemployed by reason of lack of suitable work. The able to work, available for work,
and actively seeking work requirements implement this design by testing whether
the fact that an individual did not work for any week was involuntary due to the
unavailability of suitable work.9

As a self-employed individual, the claimant is not eligible for regular unemployment
insurance benefits, but Section 2102 of the Coronavirus Aid, Relief, and Economic
Security (CARES) Act of 2020 created a new temporary federal program, Pandemic
Unemployment Assistance (PUA), that provides benefits to some self-employed
individuals, if they meet the definition of a “covered individual.” A “covered
individual” is someone who meets each of the following three conditions:
Condition #1: The individual is not eligible for regular unemployment
compensation (UC), extended benefits (EB), or pandemic emergency unemployment
compensation (PEUC). This includes an individual who has exhausted all rights to
such benefits, as well as an individual who is self-employed, seeking part-time
employment, lacking sufficient work history, or who is otherwise not qualified for
regular UC, EB, or PEUC. Self-employed individuals include independent
contractors and gig economy workers.
Condition #2: The individual must self-certify that he or she is otherwise able
and available to work within the meaning of applicable state law, except that the
individual is unemployed, partially unemployed, or unable or unavailable to work
because of a listed COVID-19 reason in Section 2102(a)(3)(A)(ii) of the CARES Act.
Condition #3: The individual must provide required documentation
substantiating employment or self-employment or the planned commencement of
employment or self-employment.10
The issue in this case is whether the claimant is a “covered individual” as of week
13 of 2020.
The claimant satisfied Conditions #1 and 3. She was self-employed in a cleaning
business and provided the required documentation to prove her self-employment.
The claimant also satisfied Condition #2, but only in weeks 13 through 20 of 2020,
while the complex where she cleaned was closed due to COVID-19 and the Safer at
Home Orders were in effect.
To be eligible for unemployment insurance benefits as to any given week, a
claimant must be able to work, available for work, and actively seeking work during
the week.11 “Able to work” means that the claimant maintains an attachment to the
labor market and has the physical and psychological ability to engage in some
substantial gainful employment in suitable work.12 “Available for work” means that
the claimant maintains an attachment to the labor market and is ready to perform
full-time suitable work in the labor market.13 “Full-time work” means work
performed for 32 hours or more per week.14 The claimant had voluntarily restricted
herself to part-time employment to maximize her Social Security benefits and was

thus not available for full-time work, a requirement for unemployment benefits.
However, in weeks 13 through 20 of 2020, the department was required to consider
a claimant to be available for suitable work during a public health emergency if the
claimant was quarantined under local, state or federal government direction or
guidance.
The government quarantine ended in week 20, so the claimant could have returned
to her self-employment in week 21 of 2020. She did not return to her self-
employment in that week, because she was homeschooling her grandchildren –
another restriction on her availability for full-time work. While there is a provision
regarding home-schooling children whose schools are closed – section
2102(a)(3)(A)(ii)(I)(dd) of the CARES Act – that section applies to an individual who
has primary caregiving responsibility for a child in their household. The claimant’s
grandchildren resided with their father.
So, the claimant was eligible for PUA under section 2102(a)(3)(A)(ii)(I)(kk) of the
CARES Act, which is applicable to a self-employed worker who experienced a
significant diminution of her customary or usual services because of the COVID-19
public health emergency, for weeks 13 through 20 of 2020. As of week 21 of 2020,
the claimant could not certify that she was otherwise able and available to work
within the meaning of applicable state law, except that she was unemployed,
partially unemployed, or unable or unavailable to work because of a listed COVID-
19 reason. A claimant ceases to be eligible for PUA when she no longer meets the
requirements to be a covered individual.
